source.title: OPIUM: Mitigating Steering Externalities and Over-Refusal via Dual Objective Latent Optimization
source.authors: Kavin Aravindan; Arihant Rastogi; Krishak Aneja; Aaditya Prasad; Saiyam Jain; Vaishnavi Shivkumar; P. Kumaraguru

record.tranche_reason: The study develops a steering-vector mitigation method motivated by safety externalities and over-refusal, and reports how that method performs. It does not test the claim’s fine-tuning, first-token KL, compliant-prefill, suffix, decoding, parameter-localization, or safety-deepening versions.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions early-token probability shifts and the shallow-safety hypothesis as background, but reports no measurement of token-position KL or test of bypassing an opening. Its experiments concern activation steering. The optimized OPIUM results and its ablations are comparisons of the paper’s own method and are not catalogued as claim-version results. The reported vanilla utility-steering ASR example and standard refusal-vector over-refusal results are recorded as findings outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds and evaluates OPIUM, an activation-steering sanitization method. It cites the shallow-safety hypothesis (Qi et al., 2024) in one related-work sentence. It also repeats Xiong et al.'s claim that utility vectors shift early-token probability away from refusal templates, but it measures nothing tied to it. There is no fine-tuning (V1, V2), no per-token KL (V3), no prefilling, suffix or decoding attack (V4), no weight or rank localization (V5), no test of causes (V6) and no deepening training (V7). Its baseline results concern activation steering, a different intervention from those the versions name, so they fall outside every version. The method does not rely on the shallow-safety finding as a tool, so T6/cites_only fits better than the reader's T4/uses_without_test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that optimizing steering vectors in activation space (OPIUM) reduces both steering-induced harmful compliance and refusal-vector over-refusal, improving the safety–utility tradeoff without weight updates.
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes activation steering vectors; it does not use the original fine-tuning or token-position measurement recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with model and behavior, comparison layer, and safety-loss weight λ. The authors state that Qwen and Llama respond differently to comparison-layer choice and that ASR is sensitive to λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla Corrigibility utility-vector steering raised Qwen2.5-7B HarmBench ASR from 28.7% to 45.0% (Sec 4.2.3, Fig 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign/utility activation steering can increase harmful-prompt compliance (steering externalities).

fits_no_version.finding: A standard refusal vector lowered HarmBench ASR (Qwen 32.50→14.06; Llama 25.31→15.31) and also lowered FalseReject CR and USR on both models (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal activation steering trades benign compliance (over-refusal) for lower harmful compliance.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026
record.problems: The optimization uses a restricted prompt subset (32 benign and 32 harmful prompts for the steering-externality experiments); the over-refusal evaluation uses a stratified 318-prompt FalseReject subset. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The main safety and utility comparisons are partly shown in Figure 2 without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: OPIUM and directional-ablation results in Figure 2 and the OPIUM results in Tables 1–3 are comparisons of the study’s own mitigation method or its ablations, not direct tests of a listed claim version. Figure-only results without separately stated values were not extracted.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on benign data. Benign utility steering is an activation intervention, not fine-tuning.
No per-token KL or position-wise comparison of aligned and base models. The early-token shift is cited from Xiong et al., not measured.
No compliant-prefix prefilling, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change attack.
No weight or rank localization of safety.
No test of whether the data or the training objective causes shallowness.
No training to deepen safety beyond the first tokens, and no test of its persistence.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6. The shallow-safety hypothesis appears only as related-work background, and OPIUM does not depend on it. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The vanilla-steering ASR values for the other settings are shown only in Figure 2, but they would still be fits_no_version findings.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or selected benign data.
No per-token KL measurement or aligned-versus-base comparison across response positions.
No compliant-token prefilling, adversarial-suffix, or decoding-change test.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
No test of whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
No training to deepen safety across response tokens or test of its persistence.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Applied the vanilla Corrigibility utility steering vector.
rows.note: The text gives this as an example of ASR rising severely after vanilla utility steering; it does not give the corresponding refusal rate.
rows.check: The baseline (28.7%) matches the 0.287 unsteered ASR in Tables 2–3 for the Corrigibility setup at layer 18. It differs from Table 1's 32.50% unsteered Qwen ASR, which uses a different refusal-vector setup. The rise appears under activation steering, not fine-tuning or prefilling, so no version applies.
